slides.heading: Interweaving Strings
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Recursion
slides.narration: Let's solve Interweaving Strings, a hard recursion problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Can `three` be formed by interleaving `one` and `two` keeping each one's order?
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Can three be formed by interleaving one and two keeping each one's order?

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Each prefix pair of the two strings either explains the next character of three or not, so memoise by indices.
slides.narration: Each prefix pair of the two strings either explains the next character of three or not, so memoise by indices.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Recursion choosing a or b at each step → O(2^(n+m))
slides.narration: Recursing on which string supplies the next letter is exponential. The state is just i and j, so memoising makes it n times m.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Recursive i and j into one and two
2. Next character of three must come from one or the other
slides.narration: Step by step. First, recursive i and j into one and two. Second, next character of three must come from one or the other. Third, memoise failed states. Fourth, succeed when all are used.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Is three an interleaving of one and two?
slides.narration: Can we build fralgogo by interleaving algo and frog, keeping each in order?

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: dp[i][j]: first i of one + first j of two make the first i+j of three
slides.narration: Dp i, j says whether the first i letters of one and j letters of two make the first i plus j letters of three. A cell is reachable from above if one's letter matches, or from the left if two's does.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: dp[4][4] = True
slides.narration: The bottom-right cell is true, so the answer is yes.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We check lengths, then recurse on i and j with a memo: if one's letter matches the next of three try advancing i, and if two's matches try advancing j.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n times m. Space is O of m.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Both strings may match the same letter
slides.narration: If lengths don't add up, return false immediately.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: A one-dimensional DP row is enough.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Each prefix pair of the two strings either explains the next character of three or not, so memoise by indices.
slides.narration: To recap Interweaving Strings: Each prefix pair of the two strings either explains the next character of three or not, so memoise by indices. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
